title: Iron Log
description: Most calorie trackers turn a five-second task into a search-and-scroll chore, so people give up within a week. Iron Log turns a photo of a plate into per-ingredient macros — grounded in USDA and Open Food Facts data, with an arithmetic check that keeps a fast, cheap model honest. Three-provider AI failover, deterministic forecasting, a zero-framework JS PWA; solo-built with FastAPI and Supabase, with a Play Store release planned.

caseStudy.tagline: Turn a photo of a plate into trustworthy macros — and keep a cheap model honest.
problem: Most calorie trackers fail for one reason: logging a meal takes too long. You search a database, scroll past forty near-matches, guess a portion, and repeat for every ingredient. People manage it for a week and quit.

I wanted logging a meal to cost one photo and a glance. But a photo-to-macros pipeline is only worth building if the numbers are right, and vision models are confidently wrong often enough to burn through a user's trust in a handful of bad guesses.

architecture.detail: A zero-framework JavaScript PWA takes the photo and posts it to a FastAPI backend. No build step, installable, and it still opens to your history offline.

The image goes to a fast, inexpensive vision model first. If a provider errors, rate-limits, or returns malformed output, the request falls through to the next of three providers before it gives up. One flaky vendor never takes the feature down.
Model output is reconciled against USDA FoodData Central and Open Food Facts rather than trusted directly, so per-ingredient macros come from an actual nutritional database instead of a guess.

A deterministic check re-adds the per-ingredient numbers and compares them to the reported totals. If the model's own math doesn't reconcile, the answer is rejected and re-requested. This is the piece that lets me run a cheap model without inheriting its arithmetic mistakes.

Entries land in Supabase on Postgres. A deterministic forecasting routine projects weight trend from intake history — the same inputs always produce the same projection, so the line doesn't jump between refreshes.

decisions.rationale: The backend is almost entirely JSON endpoints and orchestration of outbound API calls. FastAPI's async model fits fanning one request out to several AI providers, and I needed neither an ORM nor an admin.
decisions.tradeoff: I gave up Django's built-in auth and migrations and assembled those parts myself.

decisions.choice: Verify a cheap model rather than pay for a bigger one
decisions.rationale: A frontier model would still be wrong sometimes and cost an order of magnitude more per call. An arithmetic reconciliation check catches the failure that actually matters — numbers that don't add up — for almost nothing.
decisions.tradeoff: A strict tolerance rejects some correct answers too, so I spend a few extra calls to hold the trust bar high.

decisions.rationale: The interface is a camera button, a list, and a chart. A framework and its build pipeline would have been more moving parts than the product needed.
decisions.tradeoff: Routing and state are hand-rolled; past a certain feature count I would want a framework back.

decisions.rationale: People check their trend constantly. If it shifts when the underlying data did not, the whole feature feels broken.
decisions.tradeoff: A probabilistic model could show uncertainty bands, which strict determinism gives up.

caseStudy.status: Solo-built. Live on the web, with a Play Store release planned.

title: Commons
description: Commons is a small public square: anyone can read the feed, and an account gets you posting, commenting and upvoting. Because GitHub Pages has nowhere to run FastAPI, the published build answers its own API calls in the browser — and the same end-to-end suite runs against both that and the real backend, so the demo can't quietly drift from the thing it demonstrates. JWT auth with a refresh token JavaScript can't read, Postgres full-text search, 231 backend tests at 97% coverage, and no build step anywhere on the frontend.

caseStudy.tagline: A feed anyone can read, an API nobody can talk their way into — and a demo that can't drift from either.
problem: A social feed is the CRUD app everyone writes, which is exactly why it is worth writing properly. The endpoints are the boring part. The interesting part is the rules underneath them: who is allowed to see an unpublished post, what a stolen token can still do, and whether a wrong password takes the same time to fail as an account that was never there.

There was a practical problem stacked on top of it. Portfolio work has to be clickable — but GitHub Pages serves static files and has nowhere to run FastAPI, and a live demo that opens on "can't reach the server" is worse than no link at all.

architecture.step: Read is public, write is not
architecture.detail: An optional auth dependency keeps the feed readable with no token at all, while the same query quietly applies "published, or yours" — so a draft is an access rule rather than a label the interface paints on. Someone else's draft answers 404 instead of 403, because a 403 would confirm it exists.

A 15-minute access token lives in a variable and goes out as a Bearer header. The 14-day refresh token lives in an httpOnly, SameSite cookie scoped to /auth, so no content route ever sees it and no script can copy it. Refreshing rotates both, with a short grace window — otherwise opening a second tab looks exactly like a stolen cookie.

Full-text search over title and body, so any form of a word finds every other form and a title match outranks a body match. The feed's one hot query — filter on published, sort by date — gets a composite index shaped for it, and counting votes gets its own, because the votes primary key cannot answer that question.

architecture.step: The demo is a third backend
architecture.detail: The published build reimplements the API in the browser against a seeded feed, so a static host still gets an app that posts, votes, searches and remembers you across a refresh. It says so on every visit, and one button puts it back.

The Playwright specs run twice — against a standard-library mock server and against the in-browser demo — so the site people click and the API the project ships cannot drift apart. 338 end-to-end tests, plus axe on every screen there is.

decisions.choice: Vanilla JS with JSDoc types, not TypeScript
decisions.rationale: Type checking is worth having, and tsc --noEmit reads JSDoc annotations perfectly well — it catches the same class of mistake with nothing standing between the source and the browser.
decisions.tradeoff: The annotations are wordier than TypeScript's and there are no interfaces to lean on. I would revisit at around 3,000 lines, or the moment a second person works on it.

decisions.choice: Write the API a second time, in the browser
decisions.rationale: A static host cannot run the backend, and a demo that stubs out a few fetch calls is a puppet show. Reimplementing the contract means the published site genuinely works — you can register, post, upvote, edit, delete and sign out.
decisions.tradeoff: Three implementations of one contract to keep honest. That is only survivable because the same end-to-end suite runs against all of them; without it, this would be a lie with a maintenance schedule.

decisions.choice: The refresh token in an httpOnly cookie
decisions.rationale: The earlier version kept it in localStorage and said out loud what that cost: an XSS bug walks away with the session. Moving the long-lived half somewhere JavaScript cannot read closes it — an attacker can act as you while the tab is open, and takes nothing with them.
decisions.tradeoff: Cookies bring CSRF and origin rules along with them, so the refresh route needs a nonce, and serving the frontend from 127.0.0.1 instead of localhost makes the cookie silently vanish. The demo cannot have one at all, and says so rather than pretending.

decisions.rationale: The three missing points are unminified CSS and JavaScript, fixable only with the build step this frontend exists not to have. The comments in that CSS are a real part of what the repository is for.
decisions.tradeoff: Three points on a synthetic run, against a blocking time of 0 ms and a layout shift of 0 — the two numbers a person on a phone actually feels.

caseStudy.status: Solo-built. Live as an in-browser demo on GitHub Pages, with the real API shipped from CI as a Docker image.

title: Web Automation Engine
description: A desktop automation tool with a Tkinter GUI that drives browser actions through Selenium. Uses explicit waits and background threading so the UI stays responsive during login, form submission, and file tasks.

caseStudy.tagline: A desktop GUI that drives a real browser and never freezes.
problem: Automation scripts are quick to write and painful to hand to someone else. They live in a terminal, they stall on a slow page with no feedback, and the moment you bolt a GUI on the naive way, every click freezes the window until Selenium returns.
I wanted a tool a non-programmer could actually run — log in, submit forms, move files — that stayed responsive from start to finish.

architecture.detail: A tabbed window collects credentials and task parameters. It is the only thing the user touches.
Every Selenium session runs off the main thread, so the UI event loop keeps painting, the window stays responsive, and a run can report progress or be cancelled instead of locking up.

Each step waits on a specific condition — element present, clickable, gone stale — rather than a fixed delay, so the script adapts to a slow network instead of failing on it or wasting time on a fast one.
Worker threads pass state back through a queue that the main loop drains on a timer, so no Tkinter widget is ever touched from a background thread.

decisions.rationale: The work is I/O-bound — waiting on the network and the browser — so the GIL is not the constraint, and threads share state with the GUI cheaply.
decisions.tradeoff: CPU-heavy post-processing would need a process pool, which this design does not cover.

decisions.rationale: Fixed sleeps are the number one cause of flaky automation. Condition-based waits were the single biggest reliability win in the project.
decisions.tradeoff: Every interaction needs a considered wait condition — more code up front than a one-line sleep.

decisions.choice: Ship it as a desktop app
decisions.rationale: The people who need it do not have Python installed and should not have to. A window with labelled fields is an interface they already know.
decisions.tradeoff: Packaging and cross-platform GUI quirks became my problem instead of theirs.

title: Django Restaurant Menu & Digital Ordering
description: A digital ordering system for restaurants, built with Django. Manages the cart in the session, generates QR codes for tables, and gives staff a live inventory dashboard through the Django admin.

caseStudy.tagline: QR to table, cart to kitchen — a full ordering loop on Django's built-ins.
problem: A restaurant wants diners to scan a code at the table, browse the menu, and order without an app or a waiter. Staff want to watch stock fall in real time without learning new software.
The interesting constraint was doing both without a heavy single-page app and without standing up a second system just for staff.

architecture.detail: Each table has a generated QR code carrying its table ID. Scanning drops the diner onto the menu with their table already tied to the session.
The cart lives in the Django session rather than the database. An anonymous diner needs no account, and an abandoned cart expires on its own with no cleanup job to run.
Placing an order writes ordinary Django models. From there the ORM handles order history, per-item totals, and status changes.

Inventory and live orders are run from a customised Django admin instead of a bespoke back office. Staff get search, filters, and permissions for free; I tailored the list views and actions rather than building CRUD by hand.

decisions.choice: Session cart instead of a database cart
decisions.rationale: Diners are anonymous and short-lived. Session storage removes the account step and cleans up after itself.
decisions.tradeoff: A cart does not survive switching devices mid-order — an acceptable limit for dining in.

decisions.choice: Django admin as the staff tool
decisions.rationale: The staff-facing job is exactly what admin is good at: list, filter, edit, permission. A custom dashboard would have been weeks of work for a worse result.
decisions.tradeoff: Admin styling and workflow only bend so far; a very custom staff experience would eventually outgrow it.

decisions.rationale: The menu is mostly static content with a small interactive cart. Server rendering keeps it quick on a phone on restaurant Wi-Fi and easy to reason about.
decisions.tradeoff: Richer real-time behaviour would need client-side JavaScript I chose not to add yet.

title: ODE Solver
description: A visual solver for ordinary differential equations. Uses SymPy for exact symbolic solutions and Plotly for animated, frame-by-frame plots, with Euler, Heun, and RK4 methods available in a Streamlit interface.

caseStudy.tagline: Exact solutions where they exist, numerical ones where they don't — plotted step by step.
problem: A differential equations course asks you to do two things that rarely live in one tool: find the closed-form solution when there is one, and approximate it numerically when there isn't.
I wanted a single interface where you type an equation and see both at once — the symbolic answer and the numerical curve — and can watch a method build that curve one step at a time.

architecture.detail: The input equation is parsed and handed to SymPy, which returns an exact solution when the ODE is analytically solvable, rendered in proper math notation.
Euler, Heun, and RK4 are implemented directly rather than called from a library, so every step is visible and the accuracy gap between methods is the point instead of a hidden detail.
The solver emits the solution one integration step at a time and Plotly animates it, so you watch RK4 track the true curve while Euler drifts off it.
Equation, method, step size, and interval are Streamlit controls; changing any of them re-runs the whole pipeline.

decisions.rationale: A library call returns a number, not understanding. Writing Euler, Heun, and RK4 by hand makes the truncation error visible and directly comparable between methods.
decisions.tradeoff: No adaptive step size or stiffness handling of the kind a mature library ships with.

decisions.choice: Symbolic and numerical side by side
decisions.rationale: Watching the exact solution and the approximation converge — or fail to — is the entire teaching value of the tool.
decisions.tradeoff: SymPy can be slow or return nothing for messy input, so the UI has to fall back to numeric-only cleanly.

decisions.rationale: The app is inputs, then compute, then a chart. Streamlit delivers that in a fraction of the code of a web framework and deploys in one step.
decisions.tradeoff: Fine control over layout and interaction is limited; a bespoke frontend could animate more smoothly.
